sourceNotes: Seeded from MTDM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: MTDM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The share of recurring or repeat-purchase dollars lost in a period, measured on money rather than on accounts, so one enterprise account leaving at $40,000 outweighs forty $100 customers; the gross figure ignores expansion, while the net figure subtracts upgrades from it and can read below zero.
terms.whyItMatters: A case reporting 5% of customers lost but 18% of dollars lost is telling the team the losses are concentrated in the top tier, so the retention budget belongs on key accounts rather than on a mass win-back email.

terms.definition: The reciprocal of the periodic churn rate — 1 divided by 2% monthly churn is 50 months — and the multiplier that turns monthly contribution into lifetime value; it collapses fast, because moving churn from 2% to 4% halves the horizon and halves what a customer is worth bidding for.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand the team a monthly churn percentage and ask what may be spent to acquire a customer are solved by converting churn into months first; skip that step and the acquisition ceiling is a guess.

terms.definition: Contribution dollars traced back to the month a group of customers was acquired, so every acquisition class is judged on the margin it eventually returns against the acquisition spend it consumed; a cohort is profitable only once cumulative contribution crosses the cost that bought it, which pooled monthly revenue can never show.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case shows revenue rising while the newest cohorts return less contribution than older ones, the recommendation is to cut spend on the channel feeding them — and only cohort-level contribution exposes that.

terms.definition: Of the buyers who tried a product in a defined window, the percentage that bought it at least once more, counted on buyers rather than on transactions; 40% trial with 15% repeat is a very different business from 10% trial with 60% repeat, because only the second builds a base.
terms.whyItMatters: In a new-product case this number decides whether the fix is more sampling or a reformulation: weak repeat after strong trial means the product disappointed, and more advertising only buys more disappointed triers.

terms.definition: Splitting a volume change into how many households bought at all and how much each buying household took, since volume equals penetration times buying rate; a 6% decline driven by penetration falling from 12% to 11% is a lost-buyers problem, while the same decline at flat penetration is a lost-occasions problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a team that opens a declining-brand case by naming which half moved, because it picks the plan — penetration losses argue for reach and distribution, buying-rate losses argue for loyalty programs and larger packs.

terms.definition: What the next dollar in a channel returns, not what the average dollar returned — because response curves bend, a channel averaging $4.00 back can be returning $0.80 at the margin, and money should shift out of it until the last dollar spent in every channel returns the same amount.
terms.whyItMatters: Reallocation questions that list each channel's total ROI are traps: a team that pours more into the highest-average channel without asking where its curve flattened will over-fund a saturated line and starve a growing one.

terms.definition: The smallest lift a test can separate from noise at the chosen sample size and confidence level, fixed before the test runs; halving it roughly quadruples the sample required, so a two-week holdout in one small market can prove only a large effect and reports nothing for a real 2% gain.
terms.whyItMatters: Before approving a lift test in a case the team must state what size result the design can actually see, or a null read gets carried to the client as proof the campaign did nothing when the test was simply too small.

terms.definition: The sales a brand would have made in a period with no promotion or media support, estimated from de-seasonalized history, and the line every incremental claim is measured against; a promoted week running 30% above last year on a base already rising 10% on seasonality delivered 20 points of lift, not 30.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-mix output is unusable in a case until the team separates base from incremental — counting the whole promoted week as lift is the error that makes a money-losing promotion look profitable.

terms.definition: Incremental contribution margin from a retailer deal divided by the full cost of that deal, including the discount handed to units that would have sold anyway; most consumer-goods events come back below 1.0, which is why this ratio and not the volume spike is the decision number.
terms.whyItMatters: A case reporting that a promotion moved 40% more cases expects the team to net out the discount given on baseline volume and say whether the event paid, then recommend repeating, reshaping or killing it.

terms.definition: The fraction of a manufacturer's trade allowance a retailer actually converts into a lower shelf price — a $1.00 per-case allowance that moves shelf price only $0.60 passed through 60%, and the missing $0.40 became retailer margin rather than consumer demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting a deal's volume in a case requires stating this assumption out loud; assuming full pass-through overstates the lift and makes an event the team should have declined look like a winner.

terms.definition: Buyers stockpiling a discounted item they would have bought later anyway at full price, which inflates the promoted week and then digs a hole in the weeks after it; volume borrowed from the future is not incremental, so a read that stops at the spike overstates what the deal earned.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case's weekly data shows a spike followed by two soft weeks, the team should net the dip against the spike before quoting lift, or a recommendation to repeat the deal rests on volume that was never new.

terms.definition: Where a new item's sales actually come from — rivals' buyers, buyers new to the category, or the company's own existing line — and the split decides whether launch volume is worth having, because 60% drawn from a sibling brand makes most of the top line a transfer rather than growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Line-extension cases turn on this: a 500,000-unit forecast is a good result when it switches competitors' buyers and a bad one when it cannibalizes, and the judge is waiting for the team to say which.

terms.definition: A four-question survey — too cheap, cheap, expensive, too expensive — whose cumulative curves cross to bracket an acceptable price range, with the points of marginal cheapness and marginal expensiveness at the edges and the optimal price point where the two extreme curves intersect.
terms.whyItMatters: In a pricing case that supplies raw survey answers instead of a demand curve, this is the technique that converts them into a defensible price range to bring the client.

terms.definition: Purchase intent asked of one respondent at a ladder of specific prices, which produces a demand curve directly: multiplying the share still willing to buy at each price by that price locates the revenue-maximizing point, which usually sits well below the highest price anyone would still pay.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the fastest way in a roleplay to answer what to charge with a curve and a number rather than a markup rule, and it separates the revenue-maximizing price from the margin-maximizing one.

terms.definition: The score conjoint analysis assigns to each level of each attribute, so a product's appeal is the sum of its levels' scores; because price is one of the attributes, the utility gap between two features divided by the utility lost per dollar states that feature's worth in money.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-design case carrying conjoint output expects the team to convert utilities into dollars before choosing features, so the recommendation reads that the larger screen is worth $18 and costs $9, not that customers preferred it.

terms.definition: The deliberate ladder of sizes, formats and price points a brand offers, engineered so price per ounce falls as pack size rises while margin per transaction climbs; the design decides which shoppers trade up and which entry price holds the line against a cheaper rival.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases about a competitor undercutting on shelf price are usually answered by adding a smaller entry pack instead of cutting the flagship's price, and the team needs the per-unit math to prove the margin survives.

terms.definition: A year-one forecast assembled as trial households times units per trial, plus repeating households times repeat occasions times units per occasion, where the trial half is driven by awareness and distribution and the repeat half by product satisfaction — two levers that must be forecast separately.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product cases hand out awareness, distribution and repeat percentages precisely so the team can build this number and say whether the launch clears its volume hurdle.

terms.definition: The haircut applied to survey buying intent before it becomes a forecast, because stated intent overstates behavior: a common convention counts about 80% of the definitely-would-buy responses and 30% of the probably-would-buy ones, then trims again for awareness and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Handed a concept test where 45% say they would buy, a team forecasting 45% trial loses to the team that discounts intent and then multiplies by awareness and distribution to reach a number the judge can believe.

terms.definition: Campaign spend divided by the customers a holdout proves would not have bought otherwise, which runs far above blended acquisition cost because organic and returning buyers are stripped out of the denominator; it is the only acquisition figure that can honestly be set against lifetime value.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case reports $20 acquisition cost while the control group shows most of those buyers would have come anyway, the true figure may be $90 and the channel that looked cheapest is the one to cut.

terms.definition: The typical number of days between one customer's consecutive buys, which sets both when an offer should land and when silence starts to mean lapsed; in a category bought every 45 days a 60-day gap is a churn signal, while the same gap means nothing in an annually purchased category.
terms.whyItMatters: Retention plans in a case need a defensible definition of a lapsed customer, and deriving it from the category's own purchase cycle beats the arbitrary 90 days a judge will challenge.

terms.definition: The step-by-step fall from list price to the revenue actually kept, subtracting off-invoice rebates, freight and stocking allowances, co-op payments and early-payment terms, so two accounts on the same list price can differ by 15 points in what they really pay — leakage no invoice shows.
terms.whyItMatters: A margin-erosion case is solved by mapping the waterfall account by account and closing the biggest off-invoice leak, not by raising list price, which the same discounts would simply absorb again.

terms.definition: A regression over years of aggregate sales, spend, price and outside factors that estimates each channel's contribution and the bend in its response curve; it needs no user-level tracking and so survives privacy limits, but it reads slowly and cannot settle the worth of one creative.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case asks how to split next year's budget across channels, this is the evidence a team cites for the split — and knowing it requires years of variation explains why it cannot answer whether last week's email worked.

terms.definition: Setting spend by naming the marketing objective, listing every task required to reach it and costing those tasks, so the budget is built upward from what the goal demands rather than downward from a share of last year's revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify a budget request to a skeptical CFO in a roleplay, the team that prices the tasks needed to hit a stated share goal outperforms the team that cites a percentage of sales.

terms.definition: A grid of where each brand's buyers came from and went to between two periods, the diagonal holding those who stayed loyal and the off-diagonal cells showing gains and losses rival by rival, which names the one competitor a plan is actually fighting.
terms.whyItMatters: In a share-loss case it turns we lost two points into we lost them to one rival on price, which is the difference between a vague recommendation and a targeted one.

terms.definition: A pre-launch method in which recruited shoppers see advertising and a mock shelf, buy or decline, take product home and are re-contacted for repeat intent, producing a volume estimate in weeks without exposing the launch plan to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case's timeline or secrecy rules out a real city test, this is the method to propose, and knowing it forecasts trial and repeat rather than measuring real sales keeps the team honest about how firm the number is.

terms.definition: A research design in which each respondent evaluates only one version — one price, one concept, one package — so the rating is uncontaminated by side-by-side comparison; it burns more sample than a comparative design but yields numbers that behave like real-world exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting concept-test results in a roleplay, the team must say whether respondents saw one option or all of them, because sequential comparison inflates preference for the cheaper option and flatters the wrong concept.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: Creations of the mind — such as inventions, brands, and works — protected by law.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must recognize what a business can protect and how.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: Plan language reversing commission already paid when the customer cancels or fails to pay inside a stated chargeback window — often 90 days for non-payment or the first 12 months of a subscription. Once that window closes the money is the rep's to keep, so the length of the window, not the cancellation itself, decides whether the company recovers anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics-and-compensation items ask what happens when a rep sells to a customer who churns in month two, and the answer depends on the window; a roleplay on writing a commission plan is graded on naming one.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: Under the UCC a seller sheds merchantability only with conspicuous language that actually uses the word merchantability, or with an as-is / with-all-faults notice, and sheds fitness for a particular purpose only in writing. An express promise once made cannot be disclaimed at all — fine print cannot cancel what the salesperson said out loud.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a spoken performance promise with an as-is sticker and ask which survives; a product-selling roleplay is scored on not making a claim the contract cannot later walk back.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: A tax structure whose rate rises as income rises, taxing each band of income at its own rate — the opposite of a regressive tax that takes a larger share from lower earners.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-structure questions ask competitors to classify income tax, sales tax and payroll tax, and sales tax is regressive despite its single rate.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: The function that handles the individual relationship between a business and its non-union workforce — investigations, conduct issues, policy interpretation and conflict between coworkers. Labor relations, by contrast, deals with the collective relationship governed by a negotiated contract with a certified union, so a non-union employer has the first function and none of the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about building positive employer-employee relationships in a non-union business belong to this function, and misnaming it as labor relations costs the point.

terms.definition: A tiered approval ladder capping how deep each level may cut price before escalating — a rep to 10 percent, a sales manager to 20, a vice president to 30, and anything past that to finance. Margin is protected by who is allowed to sign, not by how well an individual rep negotiates, so a buyer stalling for more has to be moved up the ladder.
terms.whyItMatters: A price-negotiation roleplay where the buyer demands 25 percent off is scored on whether you know you must escalate instead of conceding; pricing items test the ladder as a control on gross margin.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: A descriptive attribute that changes over time and forces a documented choice: Type 1 overwrites the old value and loses all history, while Type 2 closes the existing row with an end date and inserts a new version row, so a sale made two years ago still ties to the sales territory that was in force on the day it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why last year's totals shifted after a store was reassigned to a new district, the answer is which of these two handling types the warehouse used.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: An inquiry the sales team has formally accepted after confirming a named need, a budget owner and a decision timeline, where a marketing-qualified lead has cleared only a behavior score such as downloads or page visits. Handoff agreements usually give sales a fixed window, often 24 hours, to accept it or send it back with a stated reason.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel items ask at which stage marketing's responsibility ends and sales' begins; a roleplay on fixing a marketing-sales dispute is scored on defining the acceptance criteria and the return window.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: An arrangement where a manufacturer reimburses part of a retailer's local advertising cost, usually on the condition that the ad features the manufacturer's brand and follows its format and logo rules, with reimbursement accrued against the retailer's purchase volume.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail roleplay where the store cannot afford a campaign alone is solved by claiming these funds, and the competitor is expected to name the strings attached rather than treat the money as unrestricted.

terms.definition: A model where reps sell entirely by phone, email and video from one location, never traveling to the customer. A field visit costs roughly five to ten times as much per contact, so firms set a deal-size floor — accounts below it are covered from the desk and only larger ones earn a visit, which is a coverage-cost decision rather than a preference.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items give a cost per contact and an average order size and ask which channel serves an account segment; a territory-planning roleplay is graded on justifying coverage by cost, not by habit.

terms.definition: Measures that protect confidential business and customer information from unauthorized access.
terms.whyItMatters: Good data security prevents costly breaches and keeps trust.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: Statutory shield for an employee who reports suspected fraud: Sarbanes-Oxley gives a retaliation complaint 180 days to reach OSHA, while Dodd-Frank pays an SEC tipster 10% to 30% of sanctions when the recovery exceeds $1 million. Reporting internally first preserves the retaliation claim but is not a precondition of the SEC award.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-ethics roleplay about a coworker's falsified expense reports, the graded answer names the channel and the filing window, not just 'tell someone'.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: The one person who controls the funds and can release them without another signature, distinct from a technical buyer who screens against specifications and can veto but never approve, and from a user buyer who judges daily impact and lives with the result. Only one of the three can say yes; either of the other two can end the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe three contacts and ask who must be reached before the close; an organizational-selling roleplay is graded on identifying who signs rather than pitching whoever answered the phone.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: The Hersey-Blanchard model matching four styles — directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating — to the follower's readiness, blending high or low task behavior with high or low relationship behavior; there is no single best style, which is what separates it from trait theories of leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay pairing one veteran and one brand-new employee is scored on assigning a different named style to each and justifying it by readiness.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: An insider with real political capital who argues the vendor's case in meetings the vendor is not invited to, and whose own standing rises if the purchase works out. A coach, by contrast, supplies intelligence and coaching on how to navigate the account but cannot spend influence or move the decision — access is not the same as power.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe a friendly contact who shares information but has no budget and ask what role that person plays; a long-cycle selling roleplay expects you to test for personal stake, not just friendliness.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: An intermediary that helps buy or sell on a producer's behalf without taking title to goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Agents lower channel cost by handling transactions without holding inventory.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: Mistakes in design or execution that distort findings and conclusions.
terms.whyItMatters: Spotting errors like sampling bias is critical to credible research.

terms.definition: Helping customers make purchase decisions through planned communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling vocabulary supports recommendations about staff, service, and revenue.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: How far sales can fall before the firm hits break-even: (actual or budgeted sales - break-even sales) / actual sales. A 12% figure means a 13% sales decline puts the operation into a loss, which is why a lender reads it next to the break-even volume rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-plan defense questions ask how risky a sales forecast is, and this ratio answers that in one number a judge can check.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: A defense under UCC section 2-302 letting a court refuse to enforce a contract or strike a single clause, and it normally demands both halves: procedural unfairness in how the bargain was struck (buried terms, adhesion, no meaningful choice) and substantive unfairness in the terms themselves (grossly one-sided price, remedy or risk allocation). A merely harsh deal freely negotiated between sophisticated parties fails the test.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-contract roleplays ask whether a court would strike a lopsided financing clause, and naming both prongs is what earns the points.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Total liabilities divided by owner's equity, showing how much of the business is financed by lenders rather than owners and how exposed it is to a downturn.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing scenarios ask whether a firm can take on another loan, and a high ratio is the reason a lender says no.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.definition: Redesigning a job by loading it vertically — handing the employee planning, decision-making and quality-checking authority previously held by a supervisor, which deepens responsibility. Job enlargement instead loads horizontally, adding more tasks at the same level of authority, and job rotation moves the person between existing jobs without changing any of them; only enrichment changes the amount of control the worker holds.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to motivate a bored experienced employee in a roleplay, adding more of the same tasks is the trap answer; the tested one is giving away supervisory decisions.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: The person accountable for the day-to-day quality, field definitions and correction of one data domain, executing rules that somebody else sets; the data owner is the business executive who sets those rules, signs off on the definitions and approves who may see the domain — accountability for the policy versus accountability for the practice.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-monitoring roleplays ask who should approve a new customer field and who should fix the 400 records already entered wrong, and the two answers are different roles.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: The opening contact and strategy used to engage a potential customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A professional approach sets the first impression that drives interest.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: Stretch of the calendar when insiders may not trade their own company's stock, typically closing two to four weeks before quarter-end and reopening one to two full trading days after earnings are released. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is the only clean way around it: trades are pre-scheduled and, under the 2023 amendments, cannot begin for at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay in which an employee wants to sell vested shares the week before an earnings release is answered by the window, not by intent.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: Number of open opportunities multiplied by average deal size multiplied by win rate, all divided by the average sales cycle length in days, which yields revenue per day: 50 x $4,000 x 0.30 / 60 days = $1,000 a day. It is the one common metric where shortening the cycle raises revenue without adding a single new prospect.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks which of four fixes lifts revenue fastest, the velocity formula shows that cutting cycle time is a divisor change and beats a small win-rate gain.

terms.definition: Comparing a specific process against a reference standard — internal across a firm's own units, competitive against a direct rival, or functional against a best-in-class firm in any industry — and importing the practice, not merely noting the score difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which benchmarking type fits a bank studying an airline's check-in speed, so the three categories have to be distinguishable.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: Petty and Cacioppo's two-route account of persuasion. An audience with both the motivation and the ability to think takes the central route, where argument quality decides and the resulting attitude is durable and resists counter-argument. An audience missing either one takes the peripheral route, where source attractiveness, the sheer length of the list and mood decide, and the attitude fades quickly. Adding more evidence for a distracted, uninvolved audience therefore changes nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A persuasive-message item that asks why a detailed cost-savings memo convinced the CFO but not the frontline staff is asking which route each audience was on.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: A distribution path where a producer sells straight to customers with no intermediaries.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct channels maximize control and margin but demand more sales and logistics effort.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: Asking questions to understand a customer's problems, goals, and requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing needs ensures recommendations truly solve the customer's problem.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: Diagnostic for redundant predictors: regress each independent variable on the others and take 1 divided by (1 minus that fit's r-squared), where anything above 5, and certainly above 10, says the predictor is so entangled with another that its individual coefficient cannot be trusted even while the overall model fits well.
terms.whyItMatters: When a model includes both ad spend and impressions and the coefficients come out with impossible signs, this is the check that explains why, and the fix is to drop or combine the tangled predictors.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.
