terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: Units of a specific add-on sold divided by units of the primary product sold, times 100 — 300 protection plans on 1,000 phones is 30%. It scores one named pairing, where cross-sell measurement counts every additional category a customer buys, so a store can raise total cross-sell revenue while this figure falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays that set an accessories goal are graded on whether you name the ratio you will move and the counter behavior that moves it, not on a general promise to sell more.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: Setting price by the value a product delivers rather than its cost.
terms.whyItMatters: It aligns price with customer benefit and market demand.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: A classical four-question procedure for locating the exact point at which two sides disagree: conjecture (did it happen?), definition (what should it be called?), quality (how serious is it?) and policy (what should be done about it?). Arguing at the wrong level is the standard failure - answering 'what should we do' while the other side is still disputing whether anything happened produces two speeches that never touch.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge in a conflict roleplay disputes your facts and you answer with a solution, you lose points for never meeting the objection; this names the level you skipped.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: Occurs when a party makes clear before performance is due that it will not perform, letting the other side treat the contract as breached at once, suspend its own performance, and sue without waiting for the due date. UCC section 2-609 adds a softer middle step: a party with reasonable grounds for insecurity may demand written assurance and suspend performance until it arrives, treating silence past thirty days as a repudiation.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a supplier emails that it probably cannot ship the spring order tests whether that is a repudiation or only grounds to demand assurance.

terms.definition: A product's characteristics and the value those characteristics give.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must separate features from benefits to sell effectively.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: A six-part qualification framework — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion — that adds the buyer's internal mechanics, the written criteria and the approval path, to the money-and-authority checks BANT stops at. It is built for long committee purchases where the signer is never the first contact.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business roleplay with a committee, naming the economic buyer and the decision criteria is the specific step judges look for before any presentation content.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: The payroll deduction funding Social Security and Medicare, taken at a fixed percentage of wages and matched dollar for dollar by the employer.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-stub interpretation items ask why gross pay minus income tax still does not equal take-home pay, and FICA is the missing line.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: A method built on teach, tailor and take control, in which the rep opens with a commercial insight that reframes how the buyer sees their own business and then respectfully pushes back on the buyer's assumptions. Relationship selling does the reverse: it builds trust first and delivers whatever the buyer already says they want.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judged on demonstrating expertise rewards teaching the buyer something about their own market, while a purely agreeable rep reads as an order taker.

terms.definition: The half of a job-analysis output that describes the person rather than the work — required education, licensure, years of experience, skills and physical requirements. Its companion, the job description, lists the duties, reporting relationship and working conditions of the position itself; a screening decision must be traceable to the specification, because a requirement that appears nowhere in it is very hard to defend as job related.
terms.whyItMatters: Building a posting in a hiring roleplay is scored on separating what the job does from what the person must bring, which is where invented requirements get caught.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.

terms.definition: The combination of hardware, software, data, and people used to collect, process, store, and share information.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding systems is key when competitors evaluate technology investments.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Connecting a product feature to the benefit the customer receives.
terms.whyItMatters: It turns product facts into customer value.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: The specific actions and tools used to carry out a marketing strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Tactics turn strategy into concrete, executable actions.

terms.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical syllogism, in which one premise is deliberately left unspoken because the audience already believes it and will supply it themselves. 'We should sponsor the tournament - our customers are all high school families' hides the premise that reaching high school families is worth what the sponsorship costs. The unstated premise is where the argument is strongest with a friendly audience and weakest with a hostile one, because attacking what was never said aloud is easier than attacking what was.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that ask what assumption a memo's recommendation rests on are asking you to recover exactly this missing premise.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: An advance paid to a rep against commission not yet earned — a $3,000 monthly draw against $2,200 of earnings leaves $800 outstanding. A recoverable draw carries that $800 forward against next month's commissions, while a non-recoverable draw forgives it, which makes the second version a guaranteed minimum in everything but name.
terms.whyItMatters: Human-resources and selling exam items ask which pay plan protects a new rep during a long ramp, and the recoverable-versus-non-recoverable distinction is the answer's hinge.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: In speech act theory (Austin and Searle), the action a speaker performs in saying something - promising, ordering, warning, refusing - as distinct from the locutionary act, which is the literal words and their sense, and the perlocutionary act, which is the effect actually produced in the hearer. 'It is cold in here' is locutionally a remark about temperature, illocutionarily a request, and perlocutionarily successful only if somebody closes the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A service roleplay in which the customer says 'I have been waiting a while' is scored on whether you answer the request rather than the sentence.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: Flat daily travel allowance that substitutes for itemized receipts — the federal standard for the continental U.S. runs near $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidentals, with the first and last travel days paid at 75% of the meal portion. Anything paid above the published rate becomes taxable wages to the traveler.
terms.whyItMatters: A hospitality or sales roleplay budgeting a three-day trip needs the arithmetic: two full days at the meal rate plus two partial days at three quarters of it.

terms.definition: A structured pitch showing how an offering meets the customer's needs.
terms.whyItMatters: A compelling presentation moves a prospect toward purchase.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: A sentence that does not describe an act but carries it out, so it cannot be true or false - only successful or void: 'I accept your offer,' 'I resign,' 'I hereby order 500 units.' Austin's felicity conditions are what make it stick - the right person, the right circumstances, the right form - which is why a casually typed 'agreed' from an authorized employee can create a binding acceptance while a long email full of enthusiasm creates nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask how a staff member bound the company in a chat message turn on this distinction between describing and doing.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: A motivation model splitting job factors into hygiene factors — pay, supervision, working conditions, policy — whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence never motivates, and motivators such as achievement, recognition, and responsibility, which alone produce satisfaction; the two run on separate scales rather than opposite ends of one.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a raise that failed to lift engagement and expect the hygiene-versus-motivator distinction as the explanation.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: A higher commission rate applied only to revenue above quota — 8% up to plan and 12% beyond it — so each dollar of overperformance pays more than the first dollar did. A cap or a decelerator does the reverse and is precisely what tempts a rep to hold a signed deal until the next period opens.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on motivating a sales force ask which plan change stops sandbagging at quarter end, and the rate structure above quota is the mechanism being tested.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: The drop in required buyer-seller contacts when an intermediary is inserted: 5 producers selling to 20 retailers need 5 x 20 = 100 direct contacts, but routing through one wholesaler needs only 5 + 20 = 25. The M x N to M + N shift, not friendliness of service, is the economic justification for paying an intermediary a margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that asks you to defend adding a wholesaler is scored on whether you can produce the contact math; judges reject the vague answer that a middleman 'saves time.'

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Responding to a customer's concerns in a helpful, persuasive way.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling objections improves trust and conversion.

terms.definition: Standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size, so precision improves far slower than the sample grows: going from 100 to 400 respondents only halves it, and going to 1,600 only halves it again. It describes how much sample means bounce around the true mean, not how spread out individual respondents are.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the quantity behind a reported margin of error, so a roleplay asking whether doubling the sample is worth the cost is answered with the square-root rule.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.

terms.definition: Measures how one product's unit sales respond to a different product's price: %change in quantity of A / %change in price of B. A positive coefficient marks substitutes and a negative one marks complements, whereas own-price elasticity compares a product only against its own price.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing roleplay about a two-item lineup asks what raising the price of one does to the other, and the sign of this coefficient is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: Sizing territories by the work each contains: accounts multiplied by the calls per year each requires, divided by the calls one rep can make — 400 accounts needing 12 calls each is 4,800 calls, and at 800 calls per rep that is six territories. The breakdown method instead divides a sales forecast by average revenue per rep and ignores how much service each account demands.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay asking you to rebalance territories after a merger wants the calculation and the service load, not an even split of the map.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: A sum the parties fix in the contract as the remedy for breach, enforceable only if two things hold: actual harm was difficult to estimate when the contract was signed, and the figure is a reasonable forecast of that harm. A number set far above probable loss is an unenforceable penalty, which throws the injured party back on proving real compensatory damages item by item.
terms.whyItMatters: Construction and event-contract roleplays ask whether a $500-per-day late clause will hold up, and the two-part reasonableness test is the answer.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: A pre-release trial run by the developer's own employees inside a controlled company setting, so defects are found before any outsider sees the product; beta testing hands the same build to real customers in their own environment, which makes who runs it and where the dividing line between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: Development-stage exam items list a testing activity and ask which stage it belongs to; the answer turns entirely on whether outsiders are involved.
